codeSnippet:
int a = 7, b = 2;
Console.WriteLine($"{a / b} {a % b} {-7 % 2}");

explanation.en: Dividing two ints truncates toward zero, so 7 / 2 is 3. The remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 % 2 is -1.
Strings are immutable. s += "d" builds a new string and points s at it; t still refers to the original "abc".
ToUpper returns a new string and leaves s untouched. The result is discarded, so s still prints "hello".

codeSnippet:
int n = 42;
Console.WriteLine($"[{n,-5}][{n:D4}][{255:X}]");

explanation.en: A negative alignment (-5) left-aligns in 5 characters, D4 pads with zeros to 4 digits, and X formats as uppercase hexadecimal.
Pt is a struct, a value type. b = a copies the whole value, so changing b.X does not affect a.

codeSnippet:
object a = 5, b = 5;
Console.WriteLine($"{a == b} {a.Equals(b)}");

explanation.en: Each 5 is boxed into its own object. == on object compares references (different boxes), while Equals compares the boxed int values.
??= assigns only when the left side is null. The first one sets "first"; the second sees a non-null value and does nothing.
Where is deferred: the filter runs only when Count() enumerates it, by which time 4 has been added. 2, 3 and 4 match.
An iterator runs lazily. The first MoveNext prints A and yields 1; the loop prints 1; the next MoveNext resumes, prints B and ends.
Switch arms are tried in order. 3.5 is a double and the when guard d > 3 holds, so the second arm wins before the plain double arm.
A positional pattern matches the tuple element by element. X is 0 and Y is anything, so (0, _) is the first arm that matches.
Records get value-based equality, so == compares X and Y. They are still two separate objects, so ReferenceEquals is false.
with copies the record and changes only Year. A record ToString prints the type name and its properties in braces, strings unquoted.

codeSnippet:
var squares = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Select(x => x * x);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", squares));

explanation.en: string.Join puts the separator ", " between each element of the sequence, with no brackets around it.
StringBuilder mutates in place and each call returns the same builder. Insert(0, "x") prepends, and 1 + 2 is evaluated to 3 before Append.
The return value is computed first, but finally runs before control leaves F. So T and F print before the caller writes 1.
The inner finally runs as the exception leaves the inner try, then the outer catch handles it, then the outer finally runs.
A static constructor runs once, just before the type is first used. Here that is the first new Cfg(), after M has printed.
Integer arithmetic is unchecked by default, so incrementing int.MaxValue wraps around to int.MinValue instead of throwing.
c++ makes c equal to B (66). c + 1 promotes to int, giving 67; casting that back to char gives C.

codeSnippet:
int? n = null;
Console.WriteLine($"{n.HasValue} {n.GetValueOrDefault()} {n + 1 == null}");

explanation.en: n has no value. GetValueOrDefault returns 0, and lifted arithmetic on null gives null, so n + 1 == null is true.
Awaiting an already-completed task does not yield: the method keeps running synchronously, so A and B print before F returns.
^1 is the last element. The range 1..3 includes index 1 and excludes index 3, giving 20 and 30.
The right-hand tuple is built first from the old values (2 and 1 + 2), then both are assigned, so a is 2 and b is 3.

codeSnippet:
int Count(params int[] xs) => xs.Length;
Console.WriteLine($"{Count()} {Count(1, 2)} {Count(new[] { 4, 5, 6 })}");

explanation.en: With no arguments params passes an empty array, not null. An existing array is passed as-is, so its length is 3.

codeSnippet: Console.WriteLine($"[{default(int)}] [{default(string)}] [{default(bool)}]");

explanation.en: default(int) is 0, default(string) is null (which interpolates as empty), and bool prints as False with a capital F.
The conditional operator is right-associative: x > 3 ? (x > 4 ? "A" : "B") : "C". Both conditions hold, so the result is A.
Since C# 5 a foreach loop variable is a fresh variable per iteration, so each lambda captures its own i.
Unlike foreach, a for loop has one i shared by every iteration. All lambdas capture it and run after the loop, when i is 3.
Remove(1) deletes the first element equal to 1, leaving 3,2,1. RemoveAt(1) deletes index 1 (the 2), leaving 3,1.
